A slack adapter lets the actuator accelerate before engagement but introduces stress-wave ringing; specimen-mounted/elastic-bar load sensing and equilibrium checks can improve data. Machine speed alone does not specify achievable specimen rate. *Bhujangrao et al.*, **DOI 10.3390/met10070894**. (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 3-5, bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 5-7, cox2013developmentofhigh pages 36-39) |
| **Drop tower / drop-bar hybrids** | A documented “**Dropkinson**” hybrid attained up to **600 s⁻¹** and about **0.27 strain** in the cited configuration; instrumentation combines impact actuation with an instrumented bar. | Useful for compression/impact and, with a special fixture, tension; pulse duration and oscillatory impact force constrain usable data. The reviewed configuration is **not** evidence of a particular commercial drop-tower manufacturer. *Bhujangrao et al.*, **DOI 10.3390/met10070894**. (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 5-7) |
| **Split Hopkinson/Kolsky bars** | Typically laboratory-built bars, striker launcher, pulse shaper, strain gauges and high-speed acquisition; compression commonly covers **>10³ s⁻¹**, with tensile and torsional variants requiring different fixtures. **NIST** used twin **1.5 m × 15 mm maraging-steel bars**, a **375 mm striker** at **9.5–13.5 m s⁻¹**, copper pulse shapers and direct-current heating; two additional tests were near **790–1,000 s⁻¹**. | Reflected/transmitted elastic waves yield specimen stress, strain and rate after dynamic equilibrium; NIST’s heated steel tests reached **1,000 °C** after approximately **3 s** heating. Its described apparatus is a research installation, **not** an Instron- or MTS-manufactured bar. *Mates et al.*, **DOI 10.1007/s40870-024-00413-1**. (cox2013developmentofhigh pages 32-36, mates2024onthedynamic pages 2-4, mates2024onthedynamic pages 4-5) |
| **Gas guns** | A gas launcher can propel the **striker of a Hopkinson bar** or, in a **separate ballistic experiment**, a projectile at a metal panel. These are distinct experiments, despite both being called “gas-gun tests.” | The retrieved sources do not reliably name a commercial *maker* for the specific metal-test launchers or justify assigning a universal projectile velocity/metal strain rate; maker identification should therefore remain **custom/not reported** rather than guessed. (cox2013developmentofhigh pages 32-36, mates2024onthedynamic pages 4-5) |

**Servo-hydraulic MTS and Instron frames** provide force-, displacement- or strain-controlled axial fatigue, creep–fatigue holds and fracture/crack-growth loading; **electrodynamic Instron ElectroPuls E3000** is explicitly documented for fatigue crack-growth testing of electrical-steel laminates. NASA’s account also identifies electromechanical **Instron** and servo-hydraulic **MTS** load frames for cyclic tests and examples of resistance, induction and quartz-lamp specimen heating. Precracked specimens and crack-length monitoring are needed for fracture-mechanics quantities; smooth-bar S–N results are not crack-growth measurements. (arnold2026developmentcharacterizationand pages 32-34, jataUnknownyearairforceresearch pages 3-5)

## 2. Creep and stress rupture

Long-duration tensile creep usually employs **dead weights and a lever arm**, a controlled multi-zone furnace, thermocouples near the gauge and an LVDT or extensometer; rupture tests run until specimen failure. An **Argonne/Idaho** report documents **four ATS 2140 direct-load frames** (rated **500 lbf**) and **two ATS 2330 20:1 lever-arm frames** (rated **10,000 lbf**). Its Alloy 617 tests covered **750–1,000 °C, 12–135 MPa**, while A508/533 tests covered **350–390 °C, 414–483 MPa**; the ATS 2961 furnace rating was **1,200 °C**. Another Argonne report identifies **ATS Series 2300** 20:1 lever-arm frames and split-tube furnaces rated **1,100 °C**. A commercial precedent is **Metcut Research** testing with **SATEC Model LD** 5:1 lever-arm creep-rupture machines. These reports do **not** establish that all stated furnace ratings were used in every creep experiment. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000018)

**Throughput means concurrent specimens, not shortened creep physics.** Argonne commissioned **nine lever-arm frames** and ran nine Alloy 709 specimens concurrently at **725 °C/140 MPa**; an earlier program reported **22 tests loaded and 10 completed**, not 22 simultaneous positions. In a different approach, an **IBERTEST-50** frame loaded **four miniature 316L specimens in series** at **650 °C**, with different sections creating different stresses and independent camera/DIC readouts; the authors describe approximately **fourfold specimen throughput** versus successive single-specimen tests, subject to pauses to remove failures. Series-loaded specimens are coupled mechanically, so that arrangement should not be represented as four independently controlled creep stations. The retrieved study supplies no verified DOI. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000016)

## 3. High strain rate, impact and non-tensile loading

| Apparatus | Makers/models actually identified and useful range | What is measured or limited |
|---|---|---|
| **High-speed servo-hydraulic** | The methods review names **Instron, MTS, Shimadzu and Zwick/Roell**. It reports an **MTS 819** hybrid arrangement with a **16 m s⁻¹** maximum machine speed and experiments near **10² s⁻¹**. Conventional frames generally serve below roughly **10 s⁻¹**, whereas intermediate-rate techniques target approximately **10–1,000 s⁻¹**. | Tension, compression, bending or shear with suitable fixtures. A slack adapter lets the actuator accelerate before engagement but introduces stress-wave ringing; specimen-mounted/elastic-bar load sensing and equilibrium checks can improve data. Machine speed alone does not specify achievable specimen rate. *Bhujangrao et al.*, **DOI 10.3390/met10070894**. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023) |
| **Drop tower / drop-bar hybrids** | A documented “**Dropkinson**” hybrid attained up to **600 s⁻¹** and about **0.27 strain** in the cited configuration; instrumentation combines impact actuation with an instrumented bar. | Useful for compression/impact and, with a special fixture, tension; pulse duration and oscillatory impact force constrain usable data. The reviewed configuration is **not** evidence of a particular commercial drop-tower manufacturer. *Bhujangrao et al.*, **DOI 10.3390/met10070894**. (pqac-00000020) |
| **Split Hopkinson/Kolsky bars** | Typically laboratory-built bars, striker launcher, pulse shaper, strain gauges and high-speed acquisition; compression commonly covers **>10³ s⁻¹**, with tensile and torsional variants requiring different fixtures. **NIST** used twin **1.5 m × 15 mm maraging-steel bars**, a **375 mm striker** at **9.5–13.5 m s⁻¹**, copper pulse shapers and direct-current heating; two additional tests were near **790–1,000 s⁻¹**. | Reflected/transmitted elastic waves yield specimen stress, strain and rate after dynamic equilibrium; NIST’s heated steel tests reached **1,000 °C** after approximately **3 s** heating. Its described apparatus is a research installation, **not** an Instron- or MTS-manufactured bar. *Mates et al.*, **DOI 10.1007/s40870-024-00413-1**. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000052) |
| **Gas guns** | A gas launcher can propel the **striker of a Hopkinson bar** or, in a **separate ballistic experiment**, a projectile at a metal panel. These are distinct experiments, despite both being called “gas-gun tests.” | The retrieved sources do not reliably name a commercial *maker* for the specific metal-test launchers or justify assigning a universal projectile velocity/metal strain rate; maker identification should therefore remain **custom/not reported** rather than guessed. (pqac-00000022, pqac-00000052) |

## 4. Fatigue and fracture

**Servo-hydraulic MTS and Instron frames** provide force-, displacement- or strain-controlled axial fatigue, creep–fatigue holds and fracture/crack-growth loading; **electrodynamic Instron ElectroPuls E3000** is explicitly documented for fatigue crack-growth testing of electrical-steel laminates. NASA’s account also identifies electromechanical **Instron** and servo-hydraulic **MTS** load frames for cyclic tests and examples of resistance, induction and quartz-lamp specimen heating. Precracked specimens and crack-length monitoring are needed for fracture-mechanics quantities; smooth-bar S–N results are not crack-growth measurements. (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046)

At higher cycling frequencies, **RUMUL Testronic** resonant machines were used at **95 Hz** in a steel comparison; **BOKU Vienna** ultrasonic equipment ran at **20 kHz**, and **Shimadzu USF-2000** is another specifically named **20-kHz** metal-fatigue machine. At 20 kHz, **10⁹ cycles require 13.9 hours of uninterrupted cycling**, versus **579 days at 20 Hz** (calculated as cycles/frequency). This is potential cycle throughput, **not** proof of equivalence: strain-rate/frequency sensitivity and self-heating must be assessed. One ultrasonic steel study used pulse–pause operation, compressed-air cooling and IR monitoring to keep the specimen at **20 ± 5 °C**. *Krupp and Giertler*, **DOI 10.3390/met12111815**; *Yamaura et al.*, **DOI 10.4236/ojmetal.2014.43007**; *Seleznev et al.*, **DOI 10.1111/ffe.13252**. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027, pqac-00000029)

## 5. Small specimens and indentation

* **Small punch:** Clamp an approximately **9.5-mm-diameter, 0.5-mm-thick disc** between dies and press its centre with a hemispherical punch; use a furnace, near-disc thermocouples, inert atmosphere and displacement transducers for creep. **Swansea University/Swansea Materials Research & Testing** built a weighted-load rig with a **2-mm alumina punch** and demonstrated CM247LC creep tests at **950 ± 1 °C, 150 N** under argon. This is an **in-house** rig, not a verified off-the-shelf Swansea-manufactured instrument. Small-punch load/deflection is not automatically a conventional uniaxial stress–strain or creep curve. *Hilal et al.*, **DOI 10.3390/ma12091390**. (pqac-00000050)
* **High-temperature nanoindentation:** **Bruker Hysitron TI980 with xSOL 800** hot stage was used on iron through **500 °C**, with heated sample/tip surroundings, **95% N₂/5% H₂** forming gas, an oxidation barrier at elevated temperature and drift control. Tests used up to **250 mN** and repeated **6–9 indents per condition**; the *tested* upper temperature is 500 °C, not the “800” in the stage name. *Khvan et al.*, **DOI 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2022.153815**. (pqac-00000040, pqac-00000041)
* **Profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP):** **Plastometrex** indents with a relatively large spherical ball, profiles the *residual* imprint and inversely fits finite-element simulations to estimate a metallic stress–strain curve; it is neither Berkovich nanoindentation nor a direct tensile/creep test. Commercial high-temperature PIP was demonstrated to **800 °C**, with approximately **10 min heat-up, 20 s indentation and 20 min cooling**. The hot-block thermocouple may differ from the specimen surface by **tens of degrees, occasionally 100 °C**, necessitating a material/geometry-specific thermal correction; oxidation and creep can bias inferred curves. *Clyne et al.*, **DOI 10.1002/adem.202100437**; *Tammpere et al.*, **DOI 10.1002/adem.202301073**. (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000034, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037)

## 6. Documented facilities, economics and evidence limits

**NASA Glenn** explicitly reports tension, creep, fatigue and crack-growth tests on ME3 disk alloy: tensile **75–1,500 °F**, creep **1,200–1,500 °F**, low-cycle fatigue **75–1,400 °F** and cyclic crack growth **75–1,500 °F**. A later **NASA Glenn–Metcut Research** GRX-810 campaign reports tension through **1,093 °C** and creep rupture at **1,093 °C**. **NASA Lewis** (the historical predecessor of Glenn), not Langley, documented ±20-kip uniaxial, tension–torsion biaxial, induction-heated and quartz-lamp systems; an example thermomechanical cycle spanned **395–606 °C**. *Gradl et al.*, **DOI 10.2514/6.2024-0997**; NASA elevated-temperature methods report **DOI 10.64631/fyfj1499**. (pqac-00000047, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000058, pqac-00000045)

**AFRL:** A documented AFRL Turbine Engine Fatigue Facility-associated Ti-6242Si tensile program covered **23–650 °C** at **8.33 × 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻² s⁻¹**, at least **three replicates per condition**; this is evidence for the *reported experimental campaign*, not a comprehensive AFRL machine inventory. *Gockel et al.*, **DOI 10.1186/s40192-016-0057-0**. **NIST** has the pulse-heated Kolsky-bar steel demonstration described above. **Argonne/Idaho** document ATS creep frames, while **Swansea Materials Research & Testing**, **Metcut**, **Westmoreland Mechanical Testing & Research** and **Element Materials Technology** appear as participating commercial/specialist testing organizations in retrieved methods. **Southwest Research Institute (SwRI)** documents a ten-specimen DMLS Inconel 738LC creep/tensile investigation, but its retrieved report does **not** name the load-frame manufacturer. (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000042, pqac-00000049, pqac-00000050, pqac-00000055, pqac-00000056)

**Langley qualification and costs:** NASA report boilerplate stating that the agency’s scientific-information office was operated by **Langley** does *not* establish that Glenn’s mechanical tests took place at Langley. The retrieved evidence is insufficient to give a defensible Langley elevated-temperature-metal-test-machine inventory or a rate/temperature envelope; it should not be conflated with Glenn. Likewise, no substantiated purchase price, contract-laboratory per-test tariff or full cost-per-data-point comparison was found. The SwRI study does report approximately **US$1,000 to produce each printed Inconel 738LC specimen**—a *specimen manufacturing cost*, **not** a creep-test fee—and explains why its program restricted test count. Concurrent creep frames, four-in-series miniatures, rapid PIP and 20-kHz cycling improve different notions of throughput and cannot be compared as though they deliver identical qualification data. (pqac-00000057, pqac-00000056, pqac-00000013, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000037, pqac-00000026)

contexts.context: The excerpt documents an elevated-temperature mechanical test setup for additively manufactured GRX-810, rather than the full range of equipment categories in the question. Specimens were produced by NASA Marshall Space Flight Center on an EOS M400 DMLS system, followed by hot-isostatic treatment at 1185°C. Mechanical load was applied with an Instron 6800-TM universal testing machine using a 50 kN load cell. Heating used an Ambrell EasyHeat induction system controlled through a Yokogawa UT55A PID controller. The induction coil was optimized in COMSOL and designed to provide a relatively uniform gauge-section temperature with a ±1% gradient target; validation used a FLIR infrared camera. Temperature was measured by a Metris M322 non-contact two-color pyrometer and a FLIR A700 camera, with the latter specified as accurate to ±2% of the reading. Full-field deformation and temperature were recorded using Correlated Solutions IR 3D-DIC, consisting of two Basler 5 MP CCD cameras and the FLIR camera. High-intensity blue illumination and selective filters addressed black-body-radiation interference. A high-temperature speckle pattern used submicron iron-oxide and alumina-oxide powders in ethanol. The excerpt does not document split-tube furnaces, Gleeble/direct-resistance systems, thermocouples, creep lever-arm or multispecimen equipment, drop towers, SHPB/gas guns, resonance fatigue systems, small-punch testing, nanoindentation, indentation plastometry, or test prices/rates/throughput. Gleeble 3800 thermomechanical simulator used as both tensile machine and resistive-heating furnace. Joule heating was controlled by feedback from a K-type thermocouple welded to the specimen’s top surface, centered along the gauge length. Testing was conducted under vacuum, with chamber pressure below 0.5 torr, to limit oxidation and reduce optical interference. The setup incorporated stereo DIC, infrared imaging, blue-light LEDs, and narrow-band filters; DIC remained usable at temperatures up to 850 °C despite visible specimen glow. contexts.context: The excerpt provides a source-specific overview of methods for metals testing across strain-rate regimes, with the cited review DOI 10.3390/met10070894. Conventional load frames and standard servo-hydraulic machines are associated with quasi-static rates of ≤10^1 s−1, while the review identifies high-speed servo-hydraulic systems from manufacturers including Instron, MTS, Shimadzu, and Zwick/Roell as devices developed for intermediate-rate testing below 10^3 s−1. One high-speed machine is reported to provide actuator speeds from 1 mm/s to 20 m/s and to support dynamic tension, compression, bending, and shear. Its slack adaptor reduces grip and actuator inertia during acceleration, but sudden engagement generates high-amplitude stress waves and oscillations. The review states that servo-hydraulic measurements become unreliable above approximately 10 s−1 because inertia produces noisy, oscillatory stress–strain data. For high rates above 10^3 s−1, SHPB methods are commonly used; gas guns and Taylor impact tests are also listed for compression, while SHTB, flyer-plate impact, and expanding-ring methods address tension. The excerpt mentions drop towers, including specialized intermediate-rate systems, but does not identify Instron Dynatup or CEAST by name, provide experimentally achieved bands for individual machines, or distinguish a Kolsky gas-gun striker from a separate projectile ballistic-impact setup.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides general methodological evidence and limitations for high-speed metallic-material testing, but it does not identify or compare the specific Instron VHS 20/25, MTS Shimadzu Zwick, Instron Dynatup, CEAST, Kolsky gas-gun, or ballistic-impact systems requested. It explains that dynamic tensile tests require a slack adapter to eliminate inertia during acceleration and that the hydraulic head must operate within the machine’s constant-speed window. Sudden engagement causes system ringing; a damping joint reduces oscillation and regulates load rise time. The maximum usable strain rate is limited by the testing system’s natural frequency, and the cited draft SAE standard recommends damping above 10 s^-1, with damping effects completed before the applied load reaches 25% of yield. Valid dynamic data require dynamic stress equilibrium and homogeneous gauge-section deformation. Drawing on SHPB practice, the excerpt gives a quantitative criterion of at least three stress-wave round trips, N ≥ 3, where N depends on load-rise time, specimen length, and elastic wave velocity; larger specimens reduce N for the same rise time. High-rate load measurement is also limited by wave propagation in load cells; piezoelectric washers respond faster, while specimen-mounted dynamometer sections can reduce load oscillations. The source is Michael Cox’s 2013 thesis, DOI 10.25560/23989.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides source-specific evidence for several intermediate/high-speed metal-testing methods, but it does not identify Instron VHS 20/25, MTS Shimadzu Zwick, Instron Dynatup, CEAST, or separate projectile gas-gun ballistic-impact systems. Conventional servo-hydraulic systems become difficult to measure reliably above 50 s−1 because slack-adaptor engagement produces stress-wave ringing; filtering or SDOF corrections may remove important hardening features. A hybrid apparatus combines a servo-hydraulic machine with a split Hopkinson bar, using strain gauges near the bar loading end to obtain cleaner load data. An MTS 819 servo-hydraulic machine is reported with a maximum speed of 16 m/s, and the hybrid technique produced less oscillatory data at approximately 10^2 s−1. Its principal limitation was only 1 ms of loading time, insufficient for adequate specimen strain, motivating wave-separation modifications. The Dropkinson hybrid drop-tower/Hopkinson-bar device achieved rates up to 600 s−1, 0.5 ms loading, and strain 0.27, but impact-generated ringing could alter force and strain signals. Flywheel testing is reported up to 1000 s−1. The source is Bhujangrao et al., Metals 2020, 10, 894, DOI: 10.3390/met10070894.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides source-specific evidence for two high-speed metallic-material testing approaches, but it does not identify the Instron VHS 20/25, MTS, Shimadzu, Zwick, Instron Dynatup, CEAST, or separate ballistic-impact gas-gun systems by name. It states that the Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar (SHPB) applies uniaxial compression at strain rates on the order of 10^3 s^-1. The configuration uses a cylindrical specimen between incident and transmitted bars, with a striker bar impacting the incident bar to generate incident, reflected, and transmitted stress waves. Strain gauges measure these waveforms, from which specimen stress, strain, and strain rate are calculated. The excerpt also reports that high-strain-rate servo-hydraulic systems can operate at rates up to 10^3 s^-1. Important limitations are that SHPB stress–strain data become valid only after stress and strain-rate uniformity is established; tension testing is difficult to compare with quasi-static or intermediate-rate tests because equipment, specimen geometry, and loading differ; and dynamic-testing guidelines are not standardized, with insufficient detail on specimens, measurement, damping, and smoothing. Consequently, data from different laboratories may not be comparable. The source is Michael Cox, “Development of high strain rate mechanical testing for metallic materials,” DOI: 10.25560/23989.

contexts.context: This excerpt provides one primary experimental methods article relevant to high-frequency metal fatigue testing: Seleznev, Weidner, and Biermann, “On the formation of ridges and burnished debris along internal fatigue crack propagation in 42CrMo4 steel,” Fatigue & Fracture of Engineering Materials & Structures, 43 (2020), 1567–1582, DOI: 10.1111/ffe.13252. The study used a conventional electromagnetic-driven RUMUL Microtron resonance pulser (Rheinfall, Switzerland) at an ultrasonic test frequency of 19.5 kHz, under symmetric push–pull loading (R = −1), with stress amplitudes of 450–650 MPa. To limit thermal self-heating during ultrasonic fatigue, testing used pulse/pause operation and continuous compressed-air cooling; specimen temperature was monitored by infrared camera and maintained at 20 ± 5 °C. contexts.context: The excerpt provides limited but relevant information about an experimentally demonstrated elevated-temperature Small Punch (SP) testing fixture developed at VTT. To maintain an inert atmosphere, the design uses a stainless-steel tube, a conical welded seal, and a rubber bellow around the ceramic deflection rod. Frictionless punch movement and gas tightness are combined using a thin metallic bellow welded into the stainless-steel tube; the bellow has a 0.1 mm wall thickness and 19 mm outer diameter. Its elastic response, together with the displacement extensometers, produces a combined spring constant of 4.32 N/mm, so the resulting spring load must be compensated in the applied load. The fixture also integrates temperature and displacement measurement through a 3 mm ceramic rod containing two thermocouple-wire holes. Two 0.5 mm S-type thermocouple wires are micro-TIG welded to a thin Nimonic plate, enabling direct specimen-temperature measurement and underside deflection measurement. The excerpt does not identify a commercial fixture manufacturer, provide SP specimen geometry, report SP test temperatures, give test duration, or discuss Bruker Hysitron TI980 xSOL 800 or Plastometrex PIP systems. The cited article DOI is 10.5334/uproc.40.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes the high-temperature nanoindentation setup and measurement corrections, but it does not state the complete tested temperature range or explicitly identify the Bruker Hysitron TI980 model. Testing was performed in an xSOL chamber using Fourmier gas, specified here as 95% nitrogen and 5% hydrogen, producing a reducing atmosphere with approximately 80 ppm residual oxygen. Oxidation at 500 °C and higher was prevented using a 20 nm amorphous SiO2 coating deposited by PECVD. The sample and diamond tip were housed in a chamber heated from above and below; the tip was heated by the chamber gas and surrounding heater radiation and mounted on a thermally isolated shank, keeping sample and tip at nearly the same temperature. Because passive indenter heating can cause cold-finger thermal drift during penetration, drift compensation was achieved by heating the indenter tip with flowing gas. Temperature accuracy was about ±1 K in absolute terms, with relative accuracy as good as 0.01 K. Hardness was calculated using the Oliver–Pharr method by fitting the first unloading segment from 95% to 20%. The indenter area function and frame compliance were calibrated on fused quartz according to ISO 14577.

contexts.context: The excerpt identifies the instrument as a Bruker Hysitron TI980 high-temperature nano-mechanical testing system fitted with an xSOL 800 heating stage. The study covered room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 500°C; the tensile tests specifically used room temperature, 400°C, and 500°C, while the nanoindentation campaign is described as extending to the same upper temperature range. The stage creates a relatively uniform hot zone using ceramic heaters positioned below and above the specimen/indenter microenvironment. The sample was mechanically clamped, while the diamond tip was attached to a low-expansion, low-conductivity glass shank using high-temperature ceramic glue. The atmosphere was not vacuum or argon in this excerpt: it was a continuous flow of forming gas containing 95 at.% N2 and 5 at.% H2, selected to protect the tip and limit oxidation. At 400–500°C, a 20 nm SiO2 surface layer was added for more complete oxidation prevention. Temperature control had an absolute error of approximately 1 K and relative error of 0.01 K. Thermal drift, including the cold-finger effect caused by heat evacuation through the indenter rod, was compensated by heating the indenter tip with the flowing gas. Indents were force-controlled to 250 mN, with 5 s loading/unloading, a 2 s dwell, 50 µm spacing, and six to nine measurements per condition. The excerpt does not state the hardness calculation method or provide hardness values.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe testing equipment, manufacturers, facilities, temperature/rate ranges, costs, throughput, citations, or DOIs. It provides only failure context: metallic failure is classified as deformation, fracture, or material loss. Yield involves primarily athermal plasticity; creep is thermally activated and depends on temperature, time, and stress. Fracture includes static, dynamic fatigue, and creep rupture. Fatigue arises from cyclic plasticity and crack nucleation/growth; stress range and cycle count are key parameters. Creep rupture involves thermally activated cavity formation and linkage, while high-temperature oxidation depends on oxygen partial pressure, time, and temperature.

contexts.context: The excerpt focuses on high-temperature optical strain measurement, noting furnace turbulence, changing refractive index, and window diffraction can create optical noise; open windows worsen it. Photoelastic coatings and conventional moiré require surface attachments and are generally limited to lower temperatures (moiré demonstrated at 750°C). Holography is noncontact and ~0.3-µm sensitive but vibration-sensitive, alignment-intensive, and mainly measures out-of-plane motion. Real-time methods support closed-loop testing but usually provide average gauge-length strain. The laser interferometric strain gauge (Sharpe method) updates ~30 Hz, uses reflective Vickers-indent marks, and operated in air to 1400°C with 100–800-µm gauge length, 300-µm range, 1-µm resolution, and 2–3% error (refs. 8–12, 61, 79).

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: What equipment is used for elevated-temperature, high-strain-rate and non-tensile mechanical testing of metals, and who makes it? Cover: (1) elevated-temperature tension and fatigue: split-tube resistance furnaces, induction heating, radiant or infrared heating, and direct-resistance heating in thermomechanical simulators (Gleeble); temperature uniformity and thermocouple attachment; high-temperature extensometers (ceramic-rod contact, laser speckle, video) and high-temperature digital image correlation; (2) creep and stress rupture: dead-weight lever-arm creep frames, multi-station or multi-specimen creep machines, and their throughput; (3) high strain rate: servo-hydraulic high-speed machines, drop towers, split Hopkinson bars and gas guns, with the makers named in methods sections; (4) fatigue and fracture: servo-hydraulic and electrodynamic frames, resonant and ultrasonic (20 kHz) fatigue machines; (5) small-specimen and indentation methods: small-punch rigs, high-temperature nanoindentation and profilometry-based indentation plastometry; (6) the main documented facilities (NASA Glenn and Langley, AFRL, NIST, Southwest Research Institute, national labs) and commercial test labs, with temperature and rate ranges, and cost and throughput where reported. Give citations and DOIs.

# Equipment and providers for mechanical testing of metals

**Scope.** The ranges below are *demonstrated test conditions* unless identified as an equipment rating. A furnace’s rated temperature is not necessarily a validated specimen temperature, and an actuator speed is not itself a specimen strain rate. Published methods often name the frame and heating supplier but not the maker of a custom Hopkinson bar or gas gun. (arnold2026developmentcharacterizationand pages 32-34, bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 3-5, mates2024onthedynamic pages 4-5)

## 1. Elevated-temperature tension, fatigue and strain measurement

| Heating approach | Documented equipment and use | Temperature-control consideration |
|---|---|---|
| **Split-tube resistance furnace** | An **Applied Test Systems (ATS)** three-zone split-tube furnace, **Watlow PM** controller and **Instron 5969** frame were paired with an **Epsilon 7650A** high-temperature extensometer. Three Type-K thermocouples were welded to the specimen gauge with a **HotSpot II** welder and read using an **Omega CSi32**. Separately, **ATS 2961** three-zone split furnaces on creep frames are rated to **1,200 °C**. | Control and report *gauge* temperature, not just furnace set point; several thermocouples detect axial gradients. The cited furnace rating is not a claim that every load train and extensometer works at 1,200 °C. (pellicotte2025acceleratedmechanicaltests pages 55-59, natesan2012creeprupturetesting pages 9-13) |
| **Induction** | An **Ambrell EasyHeat** heater, **Yokogawa UT55A** control, **Metris M322** two-colour pyrometer and **FLIR A700** IR camera heated GRX-810 specimens loaded in an **Instron 6800-TM**. A coil designed using COMSOL produced an approximately **±1% gauge-temperature gradient**; tension was reported at **982, 1,093 and 1,204 °C**. | Fast, localized heating preserves optical access, but coil design, emissivity, surface-to-core gradients and measured axial uniformity matter. The ±1% is a result for this particular coil and geometry, not a generic induction specification. (pellicotte2025acceleratedmechanicaltests pages 108-113, bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 17-20) |
| **Radiant/infrared** | NASA describes **quartz-lamp heating** alongside resistance furnaces and induction. Its illustrated **Instron** furnace-equipped axial rig is capable of **1,400 °C**, while its **MTS** environmental-chamber rig accommodates vacuum or inert gas. Radiant heating should not be confused with an IR *camera*, which measures temperature rather than heating the specimen. | Establish the temperature distribution on the actual loaded specimen and assess reflected light/thermal radiation in optical strain measurements. (arnold2026developmentcharacterizationand pages 32-34, pellicotte2025acceleratedmechanicaltests pages 108-113) |
| **Direct specimen resistance/Joule heating** | **Dynamic Systems Inc. Gleeble 3800** grips pass current through the specimen. A reported Inconel 718 arrangement used a welded central Type-K control thermocouple plus thermocouples **15 mm either side**, vacuum below **0.5 torr**, and stereo DIC/IR observation to **850 °C**. **NIST** separately demonstrated direct-current pulse heating *inside a Kolsky-bar assembly* at up to **1,000 °C s⁻¹**, before impact—not a Gleeble test. | Water-cooled grips make the middle hotter than the ends; uniformity must be verified across the intended gauge. A Gleeble thermocouple’s position/attachment, and the difference between instrument temperature resolution and thermocouple accuracy, must be reported. NIST rejected runs indicating poor thermocouple attachment or inconsistent pyrometer/thermocouple readings. (blackwell2024hightemperaturemechanicalproperty pages 54-59, kuprienko2019developmentofphysicsbased pages 32-37, mates2024onthedynamic pages 4-5) |

**Extensometry.** Contact high-temperature extensometers use ceramic/quartz gauge-contact elements or knife edges to transmit movement out of the hot zone: the documented **Epsilon 7650A** has a **1-inch gauge**, up to **10% measured strain**, and is reported as ASTM E83 Class A. Another tensile setup used ceramic knife edges entering a **Severn Thermal Solutions** furnace on an **Instron 3369**; an **Instron 8862** arrangement used an **Imetrum video extensometer**. These are *strain-measurement choices*, not interchangeable temperature ratings. Laser interferometric/speckle-based optical gauges and video methods avoid hot contact but must handle window distortion, glowing surfaces, convection and stable fiducial features; the retrieved historical optical review principally examines ceramic composites, so it is not evidence that its limiting temperatures were demonstrated on metals. (pellicotte2025acceleratedmechanicaltests pages 55-59, tammpere2024profilometry‐basedindentationplastometry pages 2-2, hemann1994ahightemperature pages 10-19)

**High-temperature DIC.** One documented system combined **Correlated Solutions IR 3D-DIC**, two **Basler** cameras, a **FLIR** thermal camera, blue illumination/bandpass filters and heat-resistant iron-oxide/alumina-oxide speckles for induction-heated GRX-810. A separate Gleeble study maintained stereo DIC at **850 °C** using blue light and narrow-band filters. DIC maps strain localization rather than only average gauge strain; camera calibration, out-of-plane motion, thermal shimmer, speckle survival and distinguishing specimen temperature from camera-observed radiance require explicit checks. (pellicotte2025acceleratedmechanicaltests pages 108-113, blackwell2024hightemperaturemechanicalproperty pages 54-59, arnold2026developmentcharacterizationand pages 32-34)

## 2. Creep and stress rupture

Long-duration tensile creep usually employs **dead weights and a lever arm**, a controlled multi-zone furnace, thermocouples near the gauge and an LVDT or extensometer; rupture tests run until specimen failure. An **Argonne/Idaho** report documents **four ATS 2140 direct-load frames** (rated **500 lbf**) and **two ATS 2330 20:1 lever-arm frames** (rated **10,000 lbf**). Its Alloy 617 tests covered **750–1,000 °C, 12–135 MPa**, while A508/533 tests covered **350–390 °C, 414–483 MPa**; the ATS 2961 furnace rating was **1,200 °C**. Another Argonne report identifies **ATS Series 2300** 20:1 lever-arm frames and split-tube furnaces rated **1,100 °C**. A commercial precedent is **Metcut Research** testing with **SATEC Model LD** 5:1 lever-arm creep-rupture machines. These reports do **not** establish that all stated furnace ratings were used in every creep experiment. (natesan2012creeprupturetesting pages 9-13, zhang2021fy21statusreport pages 16-19, fingers1998creepbehaviorof pages 47-52)

**Throughput means concurrent specimens, not shortened creep physics.** Argonne commissioned **nine lever-arm frames** and ran nine Alloy 709 specimens concurrently at **725 °C/140 MPa**; an earlier program reported **22 tests loaded and 10 completed**, not 22 simultaneous positions. In a different approach, an **IBERTEST-50** frame loaded **four miniature 316L specimens in series** at **650 °C**, with different sections creating different stresses and independent camera/DIC readouts; the authors describe approximately **fourfold specimen throughput** versus successive single-specimen tests, subject to pauses to remove failures. Series-loaded specimens are coupled mechanically, so that arrangement should not be represented as four independently controlled creep stations. The retrieved study supplies no verified DOI. (zhang2023reportoncapability pages 9-14, zhang2021fy21statusreport pages 16-19, singh2026highthroughputcharacterizationof pages 58-63, singh2026highthroughputcharacterizationof pages 37-42)

## 3. High strain rate, impact and non-tensile loading

| Apparatus | Makers/models actually identified and useful range | What is measured or limited |
|---|---|---|
| **High-speed servo-hydraulic** | The methods review names **Instron, MTS, Shimadzu and Zwick/Roell**. It reports an **MTS 819** hybrid arrangement with a **16 m s⁻¹** maximum machine speed and experiments near **10² s⁻¹**. Conventional frames generally serve below roughly **10 s⁻¹**, whereas intermediate-rate techniques target approximately **10–1,000 s⁻¹**. | Tension, compression, bending or shear with suitable fixtures. A slack adapter lets the actuator accelerate before engagement but introduces stress-wave ringing; specimen-mounted/elastic-bar load sensing and equilibrium checks can improve data. Machine speed alone does not specify achievable specimen rate. *Bhujangrao et al.*, **DOI 10.3390/met10070894**. (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 3-5, bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 5-7, cox2013developmentofhigh pages 36-39) |
| **Drop tower / drop-bar hybrids** | A documented “**Dropkinson**” hybrid attained up to **600 s⁻¹** and about **0.27 strain** in the cited configuration; instrumentation combines impact actuation with an instrumented bar. | Useful for compression/impact and, with a special fixture, tension; pulse duration and oscillatory impact force constrain usable data. The reviewed configuration is **not** evidence of a particular commercial drop-tower manufacturer. *Bhujangrao et al.*, **DOI 10.3390/met10070894**. (bhujangrao2020reviewofintermediate pages 5-7) |
| **Split Hopkinson/Kolsky bars** | Typically laboratory-built bars, striker launcher, pulse shaper, strain gauges and high-speed acquisition; compression commonly covers **>10³ s⁻¹**, with tensile and torsional variants requiring different fixtures. **NIST** used twin **1.5 m × 15 mm maraging-steel bars**, a **375 mm striker** at **9.5–13.5 m s⁻¹**, copper pulse shapers and direct-current heating; two additional tests were near **790–1,000 s⁻¹**. | Reflected/transmitted elastic waves yield specimen stress, strain and rate after dynamic equilibrium; NIST’s heated steel tests reached **1,000 °C** after approximately **3 s** heating. Its described apparatus is a research installation, **not** an Instron- or MTS-manufactured bar. *Mates et al.*, **DOI 10.1007/s40870-024-00413-1**. (cox2013developmentofhigh pages 32-36, mates2024onthedynamic pages 2-4, mates2024onthedynamic pages 4-5) |
| **Gas guns** | A gas launcher can propel the **striker of a Hopkinson bar** or, in a **separate ballistic experiment**, a projectile at a metal panel. These are distinct experiments, despite both being called “gas-gun tests.” | The retrieved sources do not reliably name a commercial *maker* for the specific metal-test launchers or justify assigning a universal projectile velocity/metal strain rate; maker identification should therefore remain **custom/not reported** rather than guessed. (cox2013developmentofhigh pages 32-36, mates2024onthedynamic pages 4-5) |

## 4. Fatigue and fracture

**Servo-hydraulic MTS and Instron frames** provide force-, displacement- or strain-controlled axial fatigue, creep–fatigue holds and fracture/crack-growth loading; **electrodynamic Instron ElectroPuls E3000** is explicitly documented for fatigue crack-growth testing of electrical-steel laminates. NASA’s account also identifies electromechanical **Instron** and servo-hydraulic **MTS** load frames for cyclic tests and examples of resistance, induction and quartz-lamp specimen heating. Precracked specimens and crack-length monitoring are needed for fracture-mechanics quantities; smooth-bar S–N results are not crack-growth measurements. (arnold2026developmentcharacterizationand pages 32-34, jataUnknownyearairforceresearch pages 3-5)

At higher cycling frequencies, **RUMUL Testronic** resonant machines were used at **95 Hz** in a steel comparison; **BOKU Vienna** ultrasonic equipment ran at **20 kHz**, and **Shimadzu USF-2000** is another specifically named **20-kHz** metal-fatigue machine. At 20 kHz, **10⁹ cycles require 13.9 hours of uninterrupted cycling**, versus **579 days at 20 Hz** (calculated as cycles/frequency). This is potential cycle throughput, **not** proof of equivalence: strain-rate/frequency sensitivity and self-heating must be assessed. One ultrasonic steel study used pulse–pause operation, compressed-air cooling and IR monitoring to keep the specimen at **20 ± 5 °C**. *Krupp and Giertler*, **DOI 10.3390/met12111815**; *Yamaura et al.*, **DOI 10.4236/ojmetal.2014.43007**; *Seleznev et al.*, **DOI 10.1111/ffe.13252**. (yamaura2014ultrasonicfatigueof pages 1-3, krupp2022surfaceorinternal pages 2-5, seleznev2020ontheformation pages 3-3)

## 5. Small specimens and indentation

* **Small punch:** Clamp an approximately **9.5-mm-diameter, 0.5-mm-thick disc** between dies and press its centre with a hemispherical punch; use a furnace, near-disc thermocouples, inert atmosphere and displacement transducers for creep. **Swansea University/Swansea Materials Research & Testing** built a weighted-load rig with a **2-mm alumina punch** and demonstrated CM247LC creep tests at **950 ± 1 °C, 150 N** under argon. This is an **in-house** rig, not a verified off-the-shelf Swansea-manufactured instrument. Small-punch load/deflection is not automatically a conventional uniaxial stress–strain or creep curve. *Hilal et al.*, **DOI 10.3390/ma12091390**. (hilal2019theinfluenceof pages 3-5)
* **High-temperature nanoindentation:** **Bruker Hysitron TI980 with xSOL 800** hot stage was used on iron through **500 °C**, with heated sample/tip surroundings, **95% N₂/5% H₂** forming gas, an oxidation barrier at elevated temperature and drift control. Tests used up to **250 mN** and repeated **6–9 indents per condition**; the *tested* upper temperature is 500 °C, not the “800” in the stage name. *Khvan et al.*, **DOI 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2022.153815**. (khvan2022hightemperaturenanoindentation pages 2-5, khvan2022hightemperaturenanoindentation pages 5-6)
* **Profilometry-based indentation plastometry (PIP):** **Plastometrex** indents with a relatively large spherical ball, profiles the *residual* imprint and inversely fits finite-element simulations to estimate a metallic stress–strain curve; it is neither Berkovich nanoindentation nor a direct tensile/creep test. Commercial high-temperature PIP was demonstrated to **800 °C**, with approximately **10 min heat-up, 20 s indentation and 20 min cooling**. The hot-block thermocouple may differ from the specimen surface by **tens of degrees, occasionally 100 °C**, necessitating a material/geometry-specific thermal correction; oxidation and creep can bias inferred curves. *Clyne et al.*, **DOI 10.1002/adem.202100437**; *Tammpere et al.*, **DOI 10.1002/adem.202301073**. (clyne2024profilometrybasedindentationplastometry pages 1-3, clyne2024profilometrybasedindentationplastometry pages 19-23, tammpere2024profilometry‐basedindentationplastometry pages 8-8, tammpere2024profilometry‐basedindentationplastometry pages 1-2)

## 6. Documented facilities, economics and evidence limits

**NASA Glenn** explicitly reports tension, creep, fatigue and crack-growth tests on ME3 disk alloy: tensile **75–1,500 °F**, creep **1,200–1,500 °F**, low-cycle fatigue **75–1,400 °F** and cyclic crack growth **75–1,500 °F**. A later **NASA Glenn–Metcut Research** GRX-810 campaign reports tension through **1,093 °C** and creep rupture at **1,093 °C**. **NASA Lewis** (the historical predecessor of Glenn), not Langley, documented ±20-kip uniaxial, tension–torsion biaxial, induction-heated and quartz-lamp systems; an example thermomechanical cycle spanned **395–606 °C**. *Gradl et al.*, **DOI 10.2514/6.2024-0997**; NASA elevated-temperature methods report **DOI 10.64631/fyfj1499**. (gabb2002characterizationofthe pages 5-7, gradl2024extremetemperatureadditively pages 4-8, thompson1986hightemperaturestressstrain pages 1-3, arnold2026developmentcharacterizationand pages 32-34)

**AFRL:** A documented AFRL Turbine Engine Fatigue Facility-associated Ti-6242Si tensile program covered **23–650 °C** at **8.33 × 10⁻⁵ and 10⁻² s⁻¹**, at least **three replicates per condition**; this is evidence for the *reported experimental campaign*, not a comprehensive AFRL machine inventory. *Gockel et al.*, **DOI 10.1186/s40192-016-0057-0**. **NIST** has the pulse-heated Kolsky-bar steel demonstration described above. **Argonne/Idaho** document ATS creep frames, while **Swansea Materials Research & Testing**, **Metcut**, **Westmoreland Mechanical Testing & Research** and **Element Materials Technology** appear as participating commercial/specialist testing organizations in retrieved methods. **Southwest Research Institute (SwRI)** documents a ten-specimen DMLS Inconel 738LC creep/tensile investigation, but its retrieved report does **not** name the load-frame manufacturer. (natesan2012creeprupturetesting pages 9-13, zhang2023reportoncapability pages 9-14, fingers1998creepbehaviorof pages 47-52, mates2024onthedynamic pages 2-4, gradl2024extremetemperatureadditively pages 4-8, hilal2019theinfluenceof pages 3-5, wilkes2018creepandtensile pages 5-8, wilkes2018creepandtensile pages 1-3)

**Langley qualification and costs:** NASA report boilerplate stating that the agency’s scientific-information office was operated by **Langley** does *not* establish that Glenn’s mechanical tests took place at Langley. The retrieved evidence is insufficient to give a defensible Langley elevated-temperature-metal-test-machine inventory or a rate/temperature envelope; it should not be conflated with Glenn. Likewise, no substantiated purchase price, contract-laboratory per-test tariff or full cost-per-data-point comparison was found. The SwRI study does report approximately **US$1,000 to produce each printed Inconel 738LC specimen**—a *specimen manufacturing cost*, **not** a creep-test fee—and explains why its program restricted test count. Concurrent creep frames, four-in-series miniatures, rapid PIP and 20-kHz cycling improve different notions of throughput and cannot be compared as though they deliver identical qualification data. (gabb2002characterizationofthe pages 1-5, wilkes2018creepandtensile pages 1-3, zhang2023reportoncapability pages 9-14, singh2026highthroughputcharacterizationof pages 58-63, tammpere2024profilometry‐basedindentationplastometry pages 1-2, yamaura2014ultrasonicfatigueof pages 1-3)

info.query: What equipment is used for elevated-temperature, high-strain-rate and non-tensile mechanical testing of metals, and who makes it? Cover: (1) elevated-temperature tension and fatigue: split-tube resistance furnaces, induction heating, radiant or infrared heating, and direct-resistance heating in thermomechanical simulators (Gleeble); temperature uniformity and thermocouple attachment; high-temperature extensometers (ceramic-rod contact, laser speckle, video) and high-temperature digital image correlation; (2) creep and stress rupture: dead-weight lever-arm creep frames, multi-station or multi-specimen creep machines, and their throughput; (3) high strain rate: servo-hydraulic high-speed machines, drop towers, split Hopkinson bars and gas guns, with the makers named in methods sections; (4) fatigue and fracture: servo-hydraulic and electrodynamic frames, resonant and ultrasonic (20 kHz) fatigue machines; (5) small-specimen and indentation methods: small-punch rigs, high-temperature nanoindentation and profilometry-based indentation plastometry; (6) the main documented facilities (NASA Glenn and Langley, AFRL, NIST, Southwest Research Institute, national labs) and commercial test labs, with temperature and rate ranges, and cost and throughput where reported. Give citations and DOIs.
